statement: Three lamps stand in a row. Each lamp is on or off. Two lamps next to each other are never both on. In how many different ways can the row of lamps look?

choices.misconception: I only counted the rows with exactly one lamp on.
I forgot the row with all three lamps off.
I only crossed out the row with all three lamps on.
I counted every on-and-off row and forgot the rule about neighbours.

hints: Is it allowed for every lamp to be off?
Make a tree: first lamp on or off, then the second, then the third. Cross out a branch as soon as two neighbours are both on. Count what is left.
With no lamps on there is 1 row. With one lamp on there are 3 rows. With two lamps on, they must not touch, so only the two end lamps work. Three lamps on is never allowed.

solutions.reliable: Sort by how many lamps are on. None on: 1 way. One on: it can be the left, middle or right lamp, 3 ways. Two on: they cannot be neighbours, so they must be the two end lamps, 1 way. Three on: impossible, since neighbours would be on together. Total $1 + 3 + 1 = 5$. The idea to keep: sort the cases by size and check the rule in each case.
solutions.elegant: All 8 on-and-off rows are possible without the rule. The rows that break the rule are on-on-off, off-on-on and on-on-on, which is 3 rows. So $8 - 3 = 5$. The idea to keep: sometimes it is quicker to count the bad cases and take them away.

whyOnTest: A rule that forbids neighbours forces careful listing, and the all-off row is the case most students forget.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
